skills.description: Create a reviewable GitHub pull request from the current branch with a Conventional Commits title, a concise evidence-based body, and before/after screenshots for UI changes. Use when asked to open, create, publish, or prepare a PR.

name: antfu-create-pr
description: Create a reviewable GitHub pull request from the current branch with a Conventional Commits title, a concise evidence-based body, and before/after screenshots for UI changes. Use when asked to open, create, publish, or prepare a PR.
metadata:
  author: Anthony Fu
  version: "2026.11.10"
---

# Create Pull Request

Open a PR that a reviewer can understand from the body alone. Explain the changed behavior and why, not the list of changed files. Keep the body proportional to the change: a one-line fix gets a few sentences, a cross-module feature gets tables and diagrams.

## Workflow

1. Inspect the repo: `git status`, current branch, remotes, default branch, `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE*`, and `AGENTS.md` / `CONTRIBUTING.md` for PR rules.
2. Compute the merge base against the target branch and record the exact `base...head` range the PR publishes. If the branch is stacked on another unmerged branch, target that branch and describe only this PR's own changes.
3. Read the full diff. Separate runtime code from generated files, lockfiles, and snapshots. Trace changed code to its entry points, callers, and external boundaries so architecture claims are backed by file paths or symbols.
4. Classify the PR (feature, fix, refactor, chore, docs) and decide which optional body sections earn their place. See [pr-body](references/pr-body.md).
5. Run the checks that match the changed surfaces (focused tests, typecheck, lint). Record the exact commands and results.
6. If the diff changes user-visible UI, capture before/after evidence. See [visual-evidence](references/visual-evidence.md).
7. Review the commit history and reshape it into atomic Conventional Commits. See [Commits](#commits).
8. Write the body to a temporary file. Push the branch. Create the PR with `gh pr create --title ... --body-file ...` (add `--attach` for each screenshot; newer `gh` can upload local images and videos from the CLI, see [Attaching files with GitHub CLI](https://docs.github.com/en/github-cli/github-cli/attaching-files-with-github-cli)). Use `--draft` when checks are still running or the work is not review-ready.
9. Open the created PR and verify title, base, head, rendered tables, diagrams, and images.
10. Address review comments: fix each confirmed issue, run focused checks, push, reply with evidence, and resolve the thread.

## Title

Use Conventional Commits, matching how the repo already writes commit messages:

```text
feat(scope): add retry to upload client
fix(scope): avoid double submit on enter
refactor: extract diff parsing from cli
chore(deps): update vite to v8
docs: clarify worktree setup
```

- Lowercase, imperative, no trailing period, under ~70 characters.
- Scope is the package, module, or feature name the repo already uses. Omit it when the change is repo-wide.
- Squash-merge repos turn the title into the commit message; write it as the commit you want in history.

## Commits

Each commit does one logical thing and uses a Conventional Commits message. A reviewer should be able to read `git log --oneline` as the story of the change and review commit by commit.

```text
# Good: each commit is self-contained
feat(api): add task creation endpoint with validation
feat(ui): add task creation form component
feat(ui): connect form to api and add loading state
test(tasks): cover task creation (unit + integration)

# Bad: everything mixed together
feat: add task feature, fix sidebar, update deps, refactor utils
```

- Keep unrelated fixes, dependency bumps, and drive-by refactors out of the branch; open separate PRs for them.
- Before pushing, review the history and split or squash local commits (`git rebase -i <base>`) until each one stands alone and builds.
- Do not rewrite commits that are already pushed and under review; add new commits instead.

## Body

Required in every PR:

- `## Summary`: the problem or capability first, then what changed and why this approach. Mention if the PR is stacked and on what.
- Linked issues: one per line as a list item, e.g. `- close #123`, `- close #456`, so GitHub renders each as a pretty issue card and auto-closes it. Use `- refs #789` for issues that should stay open.
- `## User prompts`: the model and harness in use, then a short summary of what the user asked for during the session, facts only. See [pr-body](references/pr-body.md#user-prompts).
- `## Verification`: exact commands run and their results, plus anything left unverified. Show proof matched to the change type (bug: same input before and after; perf: same workload measured both sides; CLI: real output). See [Evidence by change type](references/pr-body.md#evidence-by-change-type).

Optional, only when it helps the reviewer:

- `## Change map`: table of module, before, after, reason. Use for changes across several modules or ownership boundaries. Never a raw file list.
- `## Architecture and behavior`: a Mermaid flow, sequence, or state diagram when ordering, async work, or state transitions changed. For a fix, pair a `Before` and `After` diagram at the same abstraction level.
- `## Boundaries and risks`: table of invariant, failure mode, protection, evidence. Use when there are real failure modes, migrations, or external effects.
- `## Visual changes`: before/after image table for UI changes.
- `## Rollout and follow-up`: migrations, feature flags, known gaps. State whether a gap blocks merge.

If the repo has a PR template, keep its headings and fill them; add sections above only where the template leaves room.

## Rules

- Say what is verified, what is assumed, and what is not verified. Do not write "safe", "fixed", or "backward compatible" without pointing at the evidence.
- Green CI proves only the checks CI runs. Focused tests prove only the behavior they cover.
- Do not describe inherited changes from a parent branch as this PR's changes.
- Use plain hyphens; never em dashes (U+2014) or en dashes (U+2013).
- No filler ("This PR aims to...", "comprehensive", "robust"). Start sentences with the fact.
- Do not paste tokens, secrets, user records, or full payloads into the body.
- Do not commit screenshots or other PR-only artifacts to the repo; attach them with `gh --attach` (supported by newer `gh`, no manual upload needed).
- A description conveys belief, not proof. Show the change working instead of only saying it works.
- "Before" is what is live (base branch or production), never a faked revert. Check every capture; agents can screenshot the wrong page. Use demo or sanitized data only.
- Security fixes: keep the description short and delay exploit details until release.
- If the PR was written with the help of an agent, say so in one line at the end of the body: what the human contributed (gave the task, wrote the spec, shaped the solution) and whether they have reviewed the diff yet. If not, the reviewer is the first human to look.

## Credits

Evidence-by-type, honesty rules, and review-status disclosure are adapted from Hugo Richard's [What my pull requests look like now](https://hugorcd.com/writing/what-my-pull-requests-look-like-now).

# Issue Triage

Go through the open issues and PRs of the **current repo** (`gh repo view --json nameWithOwner`) and propose clean-up actions. Maintainers decide; the agent investigates.

## Hard Rules

- **Read-only until confirmed.** Never comment, label, close, or edit before the user approves the action tables. Reads (`gh issue view`, `gh api` GET, `gh search`) are fine.
- **Every comment says it is automated by an agent.** End with a separate last line (blank line before it): `🤖 *Automated by an agent.*`
- **Comments are short and plain.** Write them in simple English (use the `simple-english` skill if available): 1-3 short sentences, active voice, no jargon, no filler. Write each comment fresh for the item. Do not reuse a fixed template. Always include the link (PR, commit, release, or canonical issue) that justifies the action.
- Only apply approved rows. If the user edits or drops rows, follow their edits exactly.
- Be conservative: when unsure, propose `keep open` (with labels if useful) instead of closing. Do not close items with active maintainer discussion, an open linked PR, or a milestone unless the user asks.
- Use plain hyphens; no em or en dashes.

## Workflow

0. **Resume.** Look for earlier digests (`gh issue list --state all --search "Triage digest in:title"`). Read the one that matches this run (the unscoped digest for a full-repo run, the digest with the same focus for a focused run). If it exists: skip items already checked, re-check the unchecked ones, and scan only items newer than its recorded range plus items with new activity since its recorded date. Keep each item's `TASKxx` code. If none matches, scan everything in scope. Also skim the other digests for codes already used and for items already tracked there (see Scoped digests).
1. **Scope.** Confirm the repo and range (default: all open items, narrowed by the digest if there is one; for large repos ask for a limit, label, or age filter). Fetch in bulk:
   ```bash
   gh issue list --state open --limit 200 --json number,title,body,author,labels,createdAt,updatedAt,comments,reactionGroups,url,milestone
   gh pr list --state open --limit 200 --json number,title,body,author,labels,isDraft,reviewDecision,closingIssuesReferences,url,reactionGroups
   gh label list --limit 200 --json name,description
   ```
2. **Learn the labels.** Read every label name and description. Only apply labels that exist. New labels (including `spam` if missing) go in the Labels table and are created only after approval. Check how maintainers labeled similar items (`gh issue list --state all --label <l>`). Compare the repo's labels with the Recommended Labels section below and note useful ones that are missing.
3. **Map references.** Collect cross-references from bodies, comments, and the timeline (`gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{n}/timeline --paginate`): `#123`, URLs, `closes/fixes`, linked PRs, cross-repo links. Treat linked items as one cluster. Do not close an issue whose fix PR is still open. Do not mark linked items as duplicates of each other.
4. **Check each item:**
   - **Already fixed/implemented.** Search merged PRs and commits (`gh pr list --state merged --search "<keywords>"`, `git log -i --grep`), changelog, docs, and current code. Find the first release with the fix (`git tag --contains <sha> --sort=version:refname | head -1`). Verify in the code, not just the title. A partial fix is not fixed: keep it open.
   - **Duplicate.** Group by symptom or request, not wording. Search open and closed issues with distinctive text (`gh issue list --state all --search "<text>"`). Pick one canonical item: linked PR > maintainer response > best repro > most reactions > oldest. Close the others into it.
   - **Spam.** Needs two or more strong signals: promo/SEO/crypto links, off-topic text, repeated identical posts, empty body with a link, bulk activity from a new account. Typos, terse text, wrong template, or non-English are not spam.
   - **Labels.** Suggest existing labels for unlabeled or mislabeled items.
   - **Low hanging fruit.** Items a maintainer can finish fast: PRs that are approved or ready with passing CI, small PRs with a clear change, typo or docs fixes, bugs with a clear repro and an obvious small fix, and requests that are small and well defined. Say why each is quick, and propose the `low hanging fruit` label for it. Skip items that are blocked, unclear, or large.
   - **Status.** For every item that is not closed in this run, record its digest marker now, while the evidence is fresh: 🚧 a PR is open for it, ❓ you could not decide, 🚨 security, ⚠️ extra notice (see Digest Issue for the full meaning), or none. Assign it a `TASKxx` code (reuse the code from the digest if it has one, otherwise the next unused number).
   - **Demand.** Count positive reactions (👍 ❤️ 🎉 🚀), negative ones, distinct commenters, "+1" comments, and folded-in duplicates. Rate `High / Medium / Low` for the repo's size and show the raw numbers. Recent activity on an old item means it is still wanted.
5. **Present the plan** as the tables below, **Stop to ask for confirmation**. Run no write command in this turn.
6. **Execute** approved rows only, one at a time: comment, then label, then close. Stop on the first API error and report it. End with a done/failed table with links.
   - Run one issue per command (comment, label, and close for that issue chained with `&&`). Do not batch many issues in one script or loop: bulk write commands can be blocked by the permission classifier. If a command is blocked, do not work around it. Split it into smaller per-issue commands, and tell the user.
   - Create approved new labels first, in their own command.
   - For rows the user adds after the tables (for example "also close #4"), write a short fresh comment in the same style and show it in the final report.
7. **Offer a digest issue.** Ask whether to create or update the digest issue (see Digest Issue). It is built from the Needs attention rows, plus the items closed in this run. Do not write it without approval.

## Recommended Labels

General labels. Map them to the repo's existing labels first (same meaning, different name). Never rename or delete existing labels.

| Group | Labels | Meaning |
|-------|--------|---------|
| Type | `bug`, `enhancement`, `documentation`, `regression` | What kind of item it is. `regression`: only appears after a new release. |
| Triage state | `pending triage`, `needs reproduction` | Where the item is stuck. |
| Resolution | `duplicate`, `invalid`, `wontfix`, `spam` | Why it was closed. |
| Priority | `p1-chore`, `p2-nice-to-have`, `p2-edge-case`, `p3-minor-bug`, `p3-significant`, `p4-important`, `p5-urgent` | How much it matters. Descriptions: p5 breaks most users and needs a release now; p4 breaks documented behavior; p3 is an edge case or a high-priority enhancement; p2 is nice to have or has a workaround; p1 changes no behavior. |
| Contribution | `low hanging fruit` | Quick for a maintainer to finish. |
| Context | `has workaround`, `bug: upstream`, `<platform> only` (e.g. `windows only`) | Extra facts that help the next reader. |
| Area | `feat: <area>` (one per major module of the repo) | Which part of the code it touches. Derive areas from the repo's directories, docs, and past issues. |
| Bot | `bot: maybe`, `bot: likely` | Suspected bot or LLM content, short of spam. |

Rules:

- Keep every label's description filled. If an existing label has none and its meaning is clear, suggest a description.
- Suggest only labels that would help *this* repo's triage: needed by items you saw, or filling an obvious gap (for example no way to mark "needs reproduction" while many issues lack a repro). Do not suggest the whole list.
- Prefer a few `feat: <area>` labels backed by real clusters of issues over many speculative ones.
- Creating labels is a write action. List them in the Labels table (as `(new label)` rows) with name, color (match the repo's palette), description, and the items that would use them. Create only after approval (`gh label create <name> --description "..." --color <hex>`), and before applying them to items.

## Comments

Short, friendly, and specific. Examples of the tone (do not copy verbatim). Each ends with the notice on its own line:

- Fixed:
  ```md
  This was fixed in #456, released in v1.2.0. Please upgrade to get it. If it still happens, comment with a repro and we will reopen.

  🤖 *Automated by an agent.*
  ```
- Duplicate:
  ```md
  This is a duplicate of #123. Please follow that issue. Tell us if it is different and we will reopen.

  🤖 *Automated by an agent.*
  ```
- Spam:
  ```md
  Detected as a spam. Sorry if this was a mistake. Let us know and a maintainer can bring it back.

  🤖 *Automated by an agent.*
  ```

Rules per type:

- **Fixed:** link the PR or commit and release, and say what to do (upgrade, enable an option, use an API). Close as completed.
- **Duplicate:** name the canonical issue and invite the author to reopen if it differs. Close as `not planned`.
- **Spam:** add the `spam` label. Say it was detected as spam, with no reasoning. Say sorry if wrong, and say we can bring it back. Put the reasoning in the table, not in the comment. Close as `not planned`.

## Action Tables

Three tables. Close and Labels rows are numbered so the user can reply "apply 1-5, skip 3". Needs attention rows carry their `TASKxx` code instead, so the user can say "do TASK03" now and in later runs. Show the full comment text in the table.

**1. Close**

| # | Item | Reason | Link (fix / canonical) | Comment |
|---|------|--------|------------------------|---------|

`Reason` is `fixed`, `duplicate`, or `spam`. Spam rows also add the `spam` label, and their reasoning stays in this table, not in the comment.

**2. Labels**

| # | Item | Add | Reason |
|---|------|-----|--------|

Include `low hanging fruit` rows here. For a label the repo does not have, add a row with item `(new label)`, the name, description, color, and which items will use it. Approved new labels are created first (`gh label create`), then applied.

**3. Needs attention** (no write action)

| Code | Status | Item | Demand | Reactions / comments | Note |
|------|--------|------|--------|----------------------|------|

`Code` is the `TASKxx` code and `Status` is the emoji marker (empty if none), both exactly as they will appear in the digest, so the digest is a copy of this table.

Put the most recommended check-them-first items at the top, ranked by importance: high demand, regressions or build-breaking bugs, security reports, security-sensitive or long-waiting PRs, and items with active unanswered discussion. Say why in `Note`. Low hanging fruits go here too, after those, with the reason it is quick.

Do not close PRs for being stale unless asked; label or flag them instead.

## Digest Issue (optional)

After the actions are applied (or when the user only wants a report), **offer** to create a digest issue that records the Needs attention results, so later triage runs can pick up from it (Resume step). The digest is a copy of the Needs attention table; do not re-derive it. Creating an issue is a write action: ask first, show the full title and body, and create it only after approval. Skip the offer if the user declined or the list is empty.

- **Title:** `Triage digest (YYYY-MM-DD)`, or `Triage digest [<focus>] (YYYY-MM-DD)` for a scoped digest (see Scoped digests). If an earlier digest with the same focus exists (`gh issue list --state all --search "Triage digest in:title"`), offer to update it (`gh issue edit`) instead of opening a new one, and keep checked items checked.
- **Overview:** start the body with a short `Status` paragraph (2-4 sentences): the overall state of open issues and PRs (rough counts, main themes or clusters, how healthy the backlog is, what is stale or blocked), then a `Recommended start` line naming the 1-3 items to do first and why.
- **Items:** one task-list line per item: ``- [ ] `TASK00` 🚧 #134 - <concise recommendation>``. Mark items already handled as `- [x]`. Keep each line to one short sentence: what to do and why (for example `review and merge, CI green, small change`).
  - **Code:** every item gets a unique `TASKxx` code (`TASK01`, `TASK02`, ... zero-padded, numbered in order of appearance) so the maintainer can say "do TASK03 and TASK07". Codes are stable: when updating an existing digest, keep each item's code, give new items the next unused number, and never reuse or renumber. Codes are unique across all digests of the repo, not per digest (see Scoped digests).
  - **Link:** the issue or PR reference (`#134`, or the full URL for another repo) right after the code and emoji.
  - **Emoji:** one status marker between the code and the link, or none if no marker applies:
    - ✅ done: already handled or fixed
    - 🚧 wip: a PR is open for it
    - ❓ unsure: the agent could not decide, needs a maintainer call
    - 🚨 security: security report or security-sensitive
    - ⚠️ extra notice: regression, breaking change, or anything else the maintainer should read first
    - Pick the most important one; omit the emoji otherwise (`` - [ ] `TASK04` #151 - ... ``).
- **Groups:** use these headings, in order, omitting empty ones:
  1. `Prioritized` - high demand, regressions, security, long-waiting items. Most important first.
  2. `Low hanging fruit` - quick wins, with the reason it is quick.
  3. `Other` - worth a look but neither urgent nor quick.
  4. `Done in this run` - items closed or fixed in this run, as `- [x]` lines with ✅ and their own code. A later run drops them once the digest has been updated again.
- **Metadata:** end the body with a block that lets a future run continue without redoing the scan:
  ```md
  ---
  - Focus: <"all", or the domain or feature, for example `router rewrite`>
  - Selection: <for a focus: how items were chosen, for example "label feat: router, keywords navigation/guard, cluster of #120">
  - Scanned: <repo>, open issues and PRs (<fetch filters used, or "all">)
  - Date: <YYYY-MM-DD>
  - Model: <model name or id>
  - Newest item scanned: #<n> (<createdAt>)
  - Counts: <n> issues, <n> PRs scanned; <n> closed, <n> labeled in this run
  ```
- **Scoped digests:** a scoped digest is a work list for one **focus**: a domain, feature, theme, or goal the maintainer is working on (`router rewrite`, `SSR hydration`, `v2 release`, `Windows support`). It is not a fetch filter. Fetch filters (limit, label, age for a large repo) only narrow what is scanned and go in the `Scanned` line; they do not make a scoped digest. Users can keep several scoped digests next to the full one.
  - The user names the focus. Pick the items by relevance across the whole backlog, not by one label: matching labels, keywords, the code area an item touches, and its reference cluster (linked issues and PRs). Include open PRs that implement the focus, and recently merged ones only when they explain an open item. Record how you chose in the `Selection` line, and list borderline items as ❓ rather than leaving them out silently.
  - Name the focus in the title and the `Focus` metadata line, using a short stable phrase. The same phrase is how the next run finds its digest, so reuse it exactly.
  - Order the groups for the focus, not the repo: what unblocks the focus first. `Recommended start` says what to do first for this focus. The `Status` paragraph describes the focus (its open work, blockers, how close it is), not the whole backlog.
  - A scoped digest only covers items in its focus. Never mark an item outside the focus as done or missing; the full digest, if any, stays untouched.
  - Codes are shared across the repo: before assigning a new code, read all digests (open and closed) and take the next number after the highest one used. If an item is already tracked in another digest, reuse its code instead of creating a second one, and add `(also in #<digest>)` to the line.
  - When the same item is checked off in one digest, mention it in the report so the user can tick it in the others; do not edit digests outside this run's scope.
- Add the same `🤖 *Automated by an agent.*` last line. Do not add labels or assignees unless asked.
- On the next run, follow the Resume step: the digest is read first, before scoping.

name: antfu-query
description: Interview the user relentlessly about a plan, decision, or idea until reaching a shared understanding, using the agent's interactive question tool (not plain text). Use when the user wants to stress-test their thinking, clarify requirements, or says "grill me" or "query me".
metadata:
  author: Anthony Fu
  version: "2026.10.31"
  source: Adapted from https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/blob/main/skills/productivity/grilling/SKILL.md
---

# Query

Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

## Ask With the Question Tool

Put every question to the user through the agent's **interactive question tool** (for example `AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code, or the equivalent in other agents; load it first if it is deferred). Do not write questions as plain text in the reply.

- Give each question 2-4 distinct, concrete options with a short description of the trade-off.
- Put your recommended answer first and mark it `(Recommended)`, so picking it accepts your recommendation. The tool adds an "Other" option for free-form answers; do not add one.
- Keep headers short. Use multi-select only when the options are not mutually exclusive.
- Batch the whole frontier into one call, up to the tool's limit per call (4 in Claude Code). If the frontier is larger, ask the most blocking questions first and the rest next round.
- If the agent has no question tool, fall back to plain text: number the questions, list the options, and state your recommended answer for each.

## Rounds

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you have not heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round, then wait for the answers before the next round.

- Each answered round reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round.
- A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round.
- Word each question so the recommended option is the natural "yes".
- Use the user's free-form "Other" answers and notes as new input: they may add or remove branches.

## Facts vs Decisions

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a question needs a fact from the environment (files, code, tools, docs), look it up yourself or dispatch a sub-agent with a fresh context window. Do not ask the user for anything you could look up.

Do not block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait. Ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait.

## Done

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Summarize the settled decisions in a short list and **do not act on them** until the user confirms you have reached a shared understanding.

# Simplify Changes

Review the **current changes** (PR branch or working tree) and cut them down to the smallest correct diff, the way a skilled developer would. The method is an **ablation study**: remove each piece, check whether anything that matters breaks, and keep only what earns its place.

Goal: clean, minimal code with the **just-right abstraction**, that is also **robust** (handles real edge cases) and **universal** (solves the general case, not only the one that triggered the change).

## Hard Rules

- **Behavior stays the same.** Simplify only. Do not add features, change public APIs, or fix unrelated issues. Report unrelated findings instead.
- **Scope is the diff.** Only touch code the change introduced or modified, plus code that must change to remove it. Do not refactor the surrounding codebase.
- **Every removal is verified.** Run the repo's tests, typecheck, and lint after each batch. If a check has no coverage for the removed piece, reason about it explicitly or keep it.
- Match the surrounding code's style, naming, and comment density.

## Workflow

1. **Get the diff.** Pick the base: PR target branch merge base (`git merge-base HEAD origin/<default>`), else `git diff HEAD` for uncommitted work. Read the full diff and the files around it. Note the goal of the change in one sentence; it is the yardstick for everything below.
2. **Inventory the pieces.** List each unit the diff adds: function, parameter, option, branch, type, file, dependency, abstraction layer, comment, test. See [Ablation Study](#ablation-study).
3. **Ablate.** For each piece, try removing, inlining, or merging it. Decide keep or cut using [Keep vs Cut](#keep-vs-cut).
4. **Apply** the cuts in small steps. After each batch run focused checks (tests, typecheck, lint). Revert a cut that breaks behavior; that piece is now proven needed.
5. **Check the result.** Re-read the final diff as a reviewer. Is each remaining line explained by the one-sentence goal? Is it still robust and general?
6. **Report.** Show a short table of what was cut or kept and why, plus the diff size before and after (`git diff --stat`). Do not commit unless asked.

## Ablation Study

For every piece in the diff, ask: *if I delete this, what concretely breaks?*

| Piece | Ablation | Keep if |
|-------|----------|---------|
| New function / helper | Inline it at the call site | Called from 2+ places, or the name explains a non-obvious step |
| Wrapper / abstraction layer | Call the underlying thing directly | It hides real complexity or a likely-to-change boundary |
| Parameter / option / config | Hardcode the only used value | A real caller needs a different value now |
| Type / interface / generic | Use the inferred or existing type | It is exported, or inference gives a worse or wrong type |
| Branch / guard / try-catch | Delete it and run tests | It guards a reachable case (real input, real failure), not an impossible one |
| New file / module | Merge it into its only consumer | It has multiple consumers or a distinct responsibility |
| Dependency | Replace with a few lines or an existing dep | It handles hard edge cases you would otherwise get wrong |
| Duplicate logic | Reuse an existing util in the repo | No equivalent exists (search first) |
| Comment | Delete it | It explains *why* (constraint, workaround, surprising choice), not *what* |
| Test | Remove it and see what is unprotected | It covers behavior or a regression nothing else covers |
| Changed lines unrelated to the goal | Revert them | Never keep drive-by edits |

## Keep vs Cut

Cut when the piece is:

- Speculative: built for a future need nobody has (extra options, hooks, plugin points, "just in case" generics).
- Redundant: repeats what the language, framework, types, or an existing util already provides.
- Defensive against the impossible: null checks on values the types or callers guarantee, fallbacks that never run, catch blocks that swallow errors.
- Indirection without payoff: one-use helpers, pass-through wrappers, classes where a function works, factories that build one thing.
- Noise: commented-out code, narrating comments, unused imports and exports, formatting-only churn.

Keep (or even add) when the piece is:

- **Robustness:** handles real edge cases (empty input, concurrency, cleanup, cross-platform paths, error propagation with context).
- **Universality:** solves the general problem instead of special-casing the reported one. If the fix hardcodes a name, path, or value from the bug report, generalize it.
- **Right-sized abstraction:** the third repetition of something gets extracted; the first and second usually do not. A good abstraction removes more code than it adds.

If an abstraction is too small, merge; if a function does several unrelated things, split. The target is neither fewest lines nor most layers, it is the fewest concepts a reader must hold.

## Smells to Look For

- A fix that patches the symptom at the call site instead of the cause.
- Special cases (`if (name === 'foo')`) where a general rule would cover them.
- Two code paths that do the same thing with small differences; unify them.
- State, flags, or caches that can be derived from existing data.
- Long parameter lists or option bags where most values are never varied.
- Types duplicated by hand when they can be derived (`typeof`, `ReturnType`, `Parameters`, utility types).
- Hand-rolled utilities that the repo, runtime, or an existing dependency already has.
- Tests that assert implementation details or mirror the code line by line.

## Report Format

```md
| # | Piece | Action | Why |
|---|-------|--------|-----|
| 1 | `parseOptions()` in src/cli.ts | inlined | one caller, 3 lines |
| 2 | `retry` option | removed | no caller passes it; default is enough |
| 3 | `try/catch` in fetchData | kept | network errors reach users; test covers it |

Diff: +142 -8 -> +61 -8. Tests, typecheck, lint pass.
```

List anything noticed but out of scope (unrelated bugs, wider refactors) separately, and leave it alone.

skills.content:
---
name: antfu
description: Anthony Fu's opinionated tooling and conventions for JavaScript/TypeScript projects. Use when setting up new projects, configuring ESLint/Prettier alternatives, monorepos, library publishing, or when the user mentions Anthony Fu's preferences.
metadata:
  author: Anthony Fu

> Reference template: [antfu/starter-ts](https://github.com/antfu/starter-ts). When scaffolding a new TypeScript project, mirror its `package.json` scripts, `eslint.config.js`, `knip.json`, `tsdown.config.ts` and workflows rather than inventing a new layout.

## Coding Practices

### Code Organization

- **Single responsibility**: Each source file should have a clear, focused scope/purpose
- **Split large files**: Break files when they become large or handle too many concerns
- **Type separation**: Always separate types and interfaces into `types.ts` or `types/*.ts`
- **Constants extraction**: Move constants to a dedicated `constants.ts` file

### Runtime Environment

- **Prefer isomorphic code**: Write runtime-agnostic code that works in Node, browser, and workers whenever possible
- **Clear runtime indicators**: When code is environment-specific, add a comment at the top of the file:

```ts
// @env node
// @env browser
```

### TypeScript

- **Explicit return types**: Declare return types explicitly when possible
- **Avoid complex inline types**: Extract complex types into dedicated `type` or `interface` declarations

### Explicitness

Favor explicit, traceable code over implicit "magic". A reader (human or agent) should be able to follow where every name comes from without running tooling.

- **Explicit imports**: Prefer explicit `import` statements. Avoid auto-imports — when a framework provides them (e.g. Nuxt/Nitro), turn them off for new projects (see [app-development](references/app-development.md)).
- **No path aliases by default**: Use relative imports (`./foo`, `../bar`). Only use path aliases (`@/`, `~/`, `#imports`, etc.) when they are *already* configured in the project; don't introduce new ones for greenfield code.

### Comments

- **Avoid unnecessary comments**: Code should be self-explanatory
- **Explain "why" not "how"**: Comments should describe the reasoning or intent, not what the code does

### Testing (Vitest)

- Test files: `foo.ts` → `foo.test.ts` (same directory)
- Use `describe`/`it` API (not `test`)
- Use `toMatchSnapshot` for complex outputs
- Use `toMatchFileSnapshot` with explicit path for language-specific snapshots

---

## Tooling Choices

### @antfu/ni Commands

| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `ni` | Install dependencies |
| `ni <pkg>` / `ni -D <pkg>` | Add dependency / dev dependency |
| `nr <script>` | Run script |
| `nu` | Upgrade dependencies |
| `nun <pkg>` | Uninstall dependency |
| `nci` | Clean install (`pnpm i --frozen-lockfile`) |
| `nlx <pkg>` | Execute package (`npx`) |

### Checking npm Package Versions

Use [`fast-npm-meta`](https://github.com/antfu/fast-npm-meta) to look up the latest version of a package — it queries a small metadata endpoint instead of downloading the full registry payload (which can be megabytes per package).

```bash
nlx fast-npm-meta version vite              # 7.3.1
nlx fast-npm-meta version "nuxt@^3.5"       # 3.5.22 — range-aware
nlx fast-npm-meta version vite nuxt vue     # multiple at once
nlx fast-npm-meta version vite --json       # JSON for scripting
nlx fast-npm-meta full vite                 # full version list + dist-tags
```

Prefer this over `npm view <pkg> version` when you only need the latest version, and over reading `package.json` from the registry directly.

### TypeScript Config

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ESNext",
    "module": "ESNext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "strict": true,
    "esModuleInterop": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "resolveJsonModule": true,
    "isolatedModules": true,
    "noEmit": true
  }
}
```

### ESLint Setup

```js
// eslint.config.js
import antfu from '@antfu/eslint-config'

export default antfu({
  type: 'lib', // or 'app' (default)
  pnpm: true, // enforce pnpm catalogs in package.json
  antislop: true, // flag redundant/duplicated AI-style code, ban explicit `any`
})
```

Always enable `antislop: true`. It requires `eslint-plugin-slop` and `eslint-plugin-sonarjs` as dev dependencies.

For detailed configuration options: [antfu-eslint-config](references/antfu-eslint-config.md)

### Knip

Use [Knip](https://knip.dev) to catch unused files, exports and dependencies — the linter only sees one file at a time.

```json
// knip.json
{
  "$schema": "https://unpkg.com/knip@6/schema.json",
  "project": ["src/**/*.ts"],
  "ignoreDependencies": []
}
```

Fix what Knip reports by deleting; only add to `ignoreDependencies` for tools invoked outside `package.json` scripts (e.g. `taze`).

### Scripts and the `ci` Gate

Every project exposes a `ci` script that runs all checks in one command:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "build": "tsdown",
    "lint": "eslint --cache",
    "typecheck": "tsc",
    "knip": "knip",
    "test": "pnpm run build && vitest",
    "ci": "pnpm run lint && pnpm run typecheck && pnpm run knip && pnpm run test --run"
  }
}
```

**Before every commit, run `nr lint --fix` to format, then `nr ci` and make sure it passes.** Do not commit with a failing `ci`; fix the root cause instead of silencing rules or adding ignores.

### Git Hooks

`simple-git-hooks` + `nano-staged`. The pre-commit hook runs the full `ci` gate; `prepare` also installs agent skills via `skills-npm`:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "prepare": "git config core.hooksPath .githooks && simple-git-hooks && skills-npm"
  },
  "simple-git-hooks": {
    "pre-commit": "pnpm i --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts --offline && pnpm run ci && pnpx nano-staged"
  },
  "nano-staged": {
    "*": "eslint --fix --no-warn-ignored"
  }
}
```

Add `.githooks` to `.gitignore` and `simple-git-hooks: true` under `allowBuilds` in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`.

### skills-npm

[`skills-npm`](https://github.com/antfu/skills-npm) symlinks agent skills shipped inside installed npm packages (and fetches those declared in a `skills` field) into the agent's skills directory on every install. Install as a dev dependency and wire it into `prepare` as above; add `skills/npm-*` to `.gitignore`. Commit the generated `skills-npm-lock.json`.

### Publishing

Prefer npm Trusted Publishing (OIDC) over `NPM_TOKEN` secrets: releases run on CI from a `v*` tag via `release.yml` with `id-token: write`, and `nr release` (`bumpp`) only bumps, tags and pushes. Details: [setting-up](references/setting-up.md#publishing-with-npm-trusted-publishing-oidc).

### pnpm Catalogs

Use named catalogs in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` for version management:

| Catalog | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `prod` | Production dependencies |
| `inlined` | Bundler-inlined dependencies |
| `dev` | Dev tools (linter, bundler, testing) |
| `frontend` | Frontend libraries |

Avoid the default catalog. Catalog names can be adjusted per project needs.

---

| Project Setup | .gitignore, GitHub Actions, OIDC trusted publishing, VS Code extensions | [setting-up](references/setting-up.md) |
| App Development | Vue/Nuxt/UnoCSS conventions, auto-import control, Storybook component testing | [app-development](references/app-development.md) |
| Library Development | tsdown bundling, pure ESM publishing, publint, API snapshots | [library-development](references/library-development.md) |
| Monorepo | pnpm workspaces, centralized alias, Turborepo | [monorepo](references/monorepo.md) |

> The skill is based on Nitro v3 (beta, 3.0.260903), generated at 2026-09-25.

Nitro is a framework-agnostic, deployment-agnostic server toolkit powered by [H3](https://h3.dev) v2, [unstorage](https://unstorage.unjs.io), and Vite/Rolldown/Rollup. It powers Nuxt and works standalone. From one codebase it builds optimized output for Node.js, Bun, Deno, Cloudflare, Vercel, Netlify, and more.

Key capabilities:
- **Filesystem routing** with H3 v2 event handlers, dynamic params, and method suffixes.
- **Route rules** for declarative caching, headers, redirects, proxying, and CORS.
- **Caching** layer (cached handlers/functions, SWR) on top of the **unstorage** KV layer.
- **Runtime config** overridable via `NITRO_*` env vars.
- **Tasks** (on-demand + scheduled/cron), **WebSockets**/SSE, a SQL **database** layer, and **OpenAPI** auto-docs.

pnpm is a fast, disk space efficient package manager. It uses a content-addressable store to deduplicate packages across all projects on a machine, and enforces strict dependency resolution by default, preventing phantom dependencies.

**pnpm v12 is a Rust rewrite** of v11: stable, and keeps v11's commands, flags, settings, and lockfile format — so most guidance here applies to both. A handful of v12 behaviors differ (git deps resolve via HTTPS, project-aware global bins, other package managers, `packageImportMethod: auto` hardlinks first on Linux) — see best-practices-migration.

**Configuration model (important):** pnpm settings live in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` (and the global `config.yaml`) using **camelCase** keys. `.npmrc` is used **only** for authentication/registry credentials, and the `pnpm` field of `package.json` is no longer read. When working in a pnpm project, check `pnpm-workspace.yaml` for settings/workspace structure and `.npmrc` only for auth. Always use `--frozen-lockfile` (or `pnpm ci`) in CI.

> The skill is based on pnpm 12.18, generated at 2026-11-05.
